summary: Adds the PATCH method to HTTP, which lets a client send just the changes to apply to an existing resource. The existing PUT method can only replace a whole document. It is a proposed standard and the origin of the widely used PATCH request.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP has a method for replacing a document completely, called PUT, but nothing for changing one small part of it. PATCH fills that gap. The client sends a set of instructions instead of the whole document, and the server applies those instructions to what it already holds.

questions: how to partially update a resource in http
subtitle: The HTTP method for changing part of a resource instead of replacing all of it.

tldr.problem: The PUT method can only replace a whole resource with a new body, and reusing it for small changes leaves proxies, caches and servers unsure what the request really meant.
tldr.mechanism: PATCH sends a patch document, a set of instructions in a format named by the request's media type, and the server applies it to the stored resource. The server must apply the whole set of changes or none of them.
tldr.outcome: There is no single patch format, so servers advertise what they accept with the new Accept-Patch response header, and the method is neither safe nor idempotent, so clients should use conditional requests to avoid clobbering someone else's change.

today: RFC 5789 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It adds the Accept-Patch response header to the permanent registry and leaves the patch document format to the server, which advertises the formats it accepts.

sections.title: Why a New Method
sections.content:
This specification defines the new HTTP/1.1 method PATCH, which is used to apply partial modifications to a resource.

A new method is necessary to improve interoperability and prevent errors. The PUT method is already defined to overwrite a resource with a complete new body, and it cannot be reused to do partial changes, because otherwise proxies and caches, and even clients and servers, may get confused as to the result of the operation. POST is already used, but without broad interoperability: for one, there is no standard way to discover patch format support. PATCH was mentioned in earlier HTTP specifications, but not completely defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a method of its own, a change to one field would have to be sent as a whole new document. That wastes bandwidth and, worse, leaves intermediaries guessing what the request means. A separate method makes the intent clear to every hop.

sections.title: What PATCH Does and What It Requires
sections.content:
The PATCH method requests that a set of changes described in the request entity be applied to the resource identified by the Request-URI. The set of changes is represented in a format called a patch document, identified by a media type. If the Request-URI does not point to an existing resource, the server MAY create a new resource, depending on the patch document type, whether it can logically modify a null resource, and permissions.

The difference between PUT and PATCH is in the way the server processes the enclosed entity. In a PUT request the enclosed entity is considered to be a modified version of the resource stored on the origin server, and the client is asking for the stored version to be replaced. With PATCH the enclosed entity contains a set of instructions describing how a resource currently residing on the origin server should be modified to produce a new version. The PATCH method affects the resource identified by the Request-URI and it also MAY have side effects on other resources, so new resources may be created or existing ones modified by the application of a PATCH.

PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent as defined in section 9.1 of RFC 2616. A PATCH request can, however, be issued in such a way as to be idempotent, which also helps prevent bad outcomes from collisions between two PATCH requests on the same resource in a similar time frame. Collisions from multiple PATCH requests may be more dangerous than PUT collisions, because some patch formats need to operate from a known base point or else they will corrupt the resource. Clients using this kind of patch application SHOULD use a conditional request so that the request fails if the resource has been updated since the client last accessed it, for example by using a strong ETag in an If-Match header. There are also cases where patch formats do not need a known base point, such as appending text lines to log files or adding non-colliding rows to database tables, and in those cases the same care is not needed.

The server MUST apply the entire set of changes atomically and never provide, for example in response to a GET during the operation, a partially modified representation. If the entire patch document cannot be successfully applied, the server MUST NOT apply any of the changes.

Three further rules follow. If the request passes through a cache and the Request-URI identifies currently cached entities, those entries SHOULD be treated as stale, and a response to PATCH is only cacheable if it contains explicit freshness information such as an Expires header or a Cache-Control max-age directive, together with a Content-Location header matching the Request-URI; a cached PATCH response can only be used to answer GET and HEAD requests and MUST NOT be used for other methods, in particular PATCH. Entity-headers contained in the request apply only to the contained patch document and MUST NOT be applied to the resource being modified, so a Content-Language header on the request would only mean that the patch document had a language, and this document does not specify a way to modify a document's Content-Type or Content-Language value through headers. Finally, there is no guarantee that a resource can be modified with PATCH, and since different patch document formats will suit different types of resource, there is no single default format that implementations are required to support; servers MUST ensure that a received patch document is appropriate for the type of resource identified by the Request-URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends instructions, not the finished document, and the server applies them to the copy it already holds. Either all the changes happen or none do, so a reader never sees half-updated content. Because the same instructions applied twice may not give the same result, clients should check that nobody else has changed the resource in the meantime.

sections.title: A Simple PATCH Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of use of a hypothetical patch document on an existing resource.

PATCH /file.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/example
If-Match: "e0023aa4e"
Content-Length: 100

[description of changes]

The successful response to an existing text file is:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Content-Location: /file.txt
ETag: "e0023aa4f"

The 204 response code is used because the response does not carry a message body, which a response with the 200 code would have. The RFC notes that other success codes could be used as well. The ETag response header field contains the ETag for the entity created by applying the PATCH, available at the location given by the Content-Location response header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows a client naming the file, saying which patch format it is sending, and adding the tag it last saw for that file. The server answers with no body and the new tag for the updated file.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
The RFC lists the known conditions under which a PATCH request can fail.

  • Malformed patch document. When the server determines that the patch document is not properly formatted, it SHOULD return a 400 Bad Request response. What counts as badly formatted depends on the patch document chosen.
  • Unsupported patch document. A 415 Unsupported Media Type response can be used when the client sends a patch document format that the server does not support for the resource identified by the Request-URI. Such a response SHOULD include an Accept-Patch response header to tell the client which patch document media types are supported.
  • Unprocessable request. A 422 Unprocessable Entity response can be used when the server understands the patch document and its syntax appears valid, but the server is incapable of processing the request. This might include attempts to modify a resource in a way that would make it invalid, for instance a modification to a well-formed XML document that would cause it to no longer be well-formed. More specific errors such as Conflicting State can be signalled with this status code, but the more specific error would generally be more helpful.
  • Resource not found. A 404 Not Found status code can be used when the client attempted to apply a patch document to a non-existent resource, but the patch document chosen cannot be applied to a non-existent resource.
  • Conflicting state. A 409 Conflict status code can be used when the request cannot be applied given the state of the resource, for example when a patch specifies changing element 'foo' to 'bar' but element 'foo' does not exist.
  • Conflicting modification. When a client uses either the If-Match or the If-Unmodified-Since header to define a precondition and that precondition failed, the 412 Precondition Failed error is most helpful to the client. That response makes no sense if there was no precondition on the request, so in cases where the server detects a possible conflicting modification and no precondition was defined, the server can return a 409 Conflict response.
  • Concurrent modification. Some applications of PATCH might require the server to process requests in the order they are received. If a server is operating under those restrictions and receives concurrent requests to modify the same resource but is unable to queue them, it can usefully indicate this error with a 409 Conflict response.

The 409 Conflict response gives reasonably consistent information to clients. Depending on the application and the nature of the patch format, the client might be able to reissue the request as it was, have to retrieve the resource content to recalculate a patch, or have to fail the operation. Other HTTP status codes can also be used under the appropriate circumstances, and the entity body of error responses SHOULD contain enough information to communicate the nature of the error to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC maps the ways a patch can fail onto the usual HTTP status codes: the document was broken, the format is not supported, the change cannot be applied, the resource is not there, or someone else got there first. Each code tells the client something different about what to do next.

sections.title: Advertising Support in OPTIONS
sections.content:
A server can advertise its support for the PATCH method by adding it to the listing of allowed methods in the Allow OPTIONS response header defined in HTTP/1.1. The PATCH method MAY appear in the Allow header even if the Accept-Patch header is absent, in which case the list of allowed patch documents is not advertised.

The specification introduces a new response header, Accept-Patch, used to specify the patch document formats accepted by the server. Accept-Patch SHOULD appear in the OPTIONS response for any resource that supports the use of the PATCH method. The presence of the header in response to any method is an implicit indication that PATCH is allowed on the resource identified by the Request-URI, and the presence of a specific patch document format in it indicates that that specific format is allowed on that resource.

The header carries a comma-separated listing of media types, with optional parameters, as defined in section 3.7 of RFC 2616, for example Accept-Patch: text/example;charset=utf-8.

The RFC gives an example request and response for a server that supports PATCH generally using two hypothetical patch document formats.

[request]

OPTIONS /example/buddies.xml HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com

[response]

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Allow: GET, PUT, POST, OPTIONS, HEAD, DELETE, PATCH
Accept-Patch: application/example, text/example
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask a server which methods and which patch formats it supports, and the server answers in its OPTIONS reply. The new Accept-Patch header lists the patch formats; the Allow header says whether PATCH itself is on offer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for PATCH are nearly identical to those for PUT, which include authorizing requests, possibly through access control and authentication, and ensuring that data is not corrupted through transport errors or through accidental overwrites. Whatever mechanisms are used for PUT can be used for PATCH as well.

Two considerations apply especially to PATCH. A document that is patched might be more likely to be corrupted than a document that is overridden in its entirety, and that concern can be addressed through conditional requests using ETags and the If-Match request header. If a PATCH request fails, the client can issue a GET request to the resource to see what state it is in; in some cases the client might be able to check the contents to see whether the PATCH can be resent, and in other cases the attempt will fail and a user will have to verify intent. In the case of a failure of the underlying transport channel, where a PATCH response is not received before the channel fails or a timeout happens, the client might have to issue a GET request to see whether the request was applied, and the client might want that GET to bypass caches.

Sometimes an HTTP intermediary tries to detect viruses sent over HTTP by checking the body of a PUT or POST request or of a GET response. The PATCH method complicates such watch-keeping, because neither the source document nor the patch document might be a virus, yet the result could be. The RFC says this is not materially different from the concerns already introduced by byte-range downloads, downloading patch documents and uploading compressed files. Individual patch documents will have their own specific security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing part of a file can damage it more easily than replacing it, so the client should say which version it is changing, and check afterwards if the request failed. A middlebox that scans for viruses also has a harder job, because neither the instructions nor the original document need be harmful for the result to be.

viz.caption: WHAT THE BODY OF EACH REQUEST MEANS

cells: The complete new version of the resource; the stored copy is replaced
Instructions describing how the stored resource should be modified
Used in widely varying ways; can encompass PUT and PATCH-like operations

data.title: A PATCH request and its response
data.code:
PATCH /file.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/example
If-Match: "e0023aa4e"
Content-Length: 100

[description of changes]

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Content-Location: /file.txt
ETag: "e0023aa4f"

data.title: Asking which patch formats are supported
data.code:
OPTIONS /example/buddies.xml HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Allow: GET, PUT, POST, OPTIONS, HEAD, DELETE, PATCH
Accept-Patch: application/example, text/example

viz.caption: THE STATUS CODES A FAILED PATCH CAN RETURN

items.label: BAD REQUEST
items.desc: The patch document is not properly formatted.

items.label: NOT FOUND
items.desc: The resource does not exist and the patch format cannot create one.

items.label: CONFLICT
items.desc: The request cannot be applied given the state of the resource, or a concurrent request was not queued.

items.label: PRECONDITION FAILED
items.desc: An If-Match or If-Unmodified-Since precondition did not hold.

items.label: UNSUPPORTED MEDIA TYPE
items.desc: The server does not support that patch format for this resource.

items.label: UNPROCESSABLE ENTITY
items.desc: The document is understood but the server cannot carry out the change.
